# QUIC and WebTransport

Before following a subscription, we need to understand what carries it. This chapter explains the transport promises a MoQ application uses, then looks inside the packets that carry them. You do not need to memorize packet headers; you need to know which layer is responsible when something is delayed or lost.

## A short introduction to TCP/IP

The Internet connects networks. A **router** forwards packets toward a destination, usually through other routers. **IP**, the Internet Protocol, supplies addressing and packet delivery across those networks. An IP address identifies a network interface; it is not a permanent identity for a person or an application.

A packet contains a **header**, which describes how to handle it, and a **payload**, the data it carries. Layers nest: the payload of an IP packet can contain a UDP datagram, whose payload contains QUIC packets. The receiving software unwraps those layers.

An address gets traffic to a host. A **port** helps the host direct that traffic to the appropriate transport endpoint. A server may listen for QUIC on UDP port 443 while serving TCP connections on TCP port 443: the transport protocol is part of the distinction. DNS translates a name such as `relay.example` into addresses the client can try. DNS resolution alone does not establish a connection.

| Term | What it identifies or carries | What it does not tell you |
|---|---|---|
| IP address | A source or destination interface | Which lecture or track the viewer wants |
| UDP or TCP port | A transport endpoint on a host | Whether the application understands MoQ |
| Packet | A unit sent across a network | Whether its payload is a complete media object |
| Connection | State maintained by communicating transport endpoints | Whether received media can be decoded |
| Protocol | Rules both endpoints follow to interpret messages | Which implementation a particular server runs |

IP delivery is **best effort**. Packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or delayed. A full queue in a router is one reason for loss. Each link has a **maximum transmission unit**, or MTU: its largest IP packet size. The **path MTU** is the smallest link MTU along the route. Sending one large application message does not make the network carry it as one arbitrarily large packet. See the [IPv6 specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200.html#section-5) for packet-size constraints.

### TCP and UDP make different promises

**TCP**, the Transmission Control Protocol, provides an ordered byte stream. It tracks bytes, acknowledges progress, and repairs loss. The application reads a continuous sequence rather than individual network packets. If the connection fails, reliable delivery does not make the missing bytes magically arrive.

**UDP**, the User Datagram Protocol, preserves message boundaries but does not supply ordering or retransmission. The application receives individual datagrams that reach it. A protocol built above UDP can add reliability, security, and congestion control. QUIC does exactly that.

| Property | TCP | UDP | QUIC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carried directly by | IP | IP | UDP |
| Application data | One ordered byte stream in each direction | Separate datagrams | Multiple ordered byte streams; optional datagrams |
| Repairs lost application data | Yes, while the connection remains viable | No | Stream data: yes. QUIC datagrams: no |
| Preserves application message boundaries | No | Yes | Streams: no. Datagrams: yes |
| Encryption built into this protocol | No; commonly combined with TLS | No | Yes; integrates TLS 1.3 |
| Congestion control | Yes | Not supplied by UDP itself | Yes, including datagram traffic |

The comparison concerns the transport service, not a speed ranking. A UDP application still needs responsible sending behavior. A TCP application can have low latency. QUIC offers a different way to organize delivery. The base specifications are [TCP, RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html), [UDP, RFC 768](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768.html), and [QUIC, RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html).

### Delay, rate, and feedback

**Bandwidth** describes a path's carrying capacity. **Throughput** is the rate actually achieved. **Latency** is delay; always name the interval being measured. Network delay and the delay from a camera capturing a picture to a screen displaying it are different measurements.

An **acknowledgment**, or ACK, tells a sender what transport data arrived. **Round-trip time**, or RTT, measures a trip to the peer and back. A sender uses feedback to estimate the path and detect possible loss. An ACK does not prove that a video decoder accepted the bytes or that a viewer saw the picture.

Two limits can stop a sender:

| Limit | Question it answers | Typical response |
|---|---|---|
| Flow control | Can the receiver accept more stream bytes? | Wait for the receiver to advertise more capacity |
| Congestion control | How much traffic can the network sustain? | Adjust the amount and pace of traffic sent |

A slow reader and a congested network can both look like “sending stopped,” but they need different fixes. QUIC's loss detection and congestion control are described in [RFC 9002](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002.html).


## Why one ordered stream can hurt

Imagine sending camera video and captions through a single ordered byte stream. A packet containing video bytes goes missing. Later caption bytes arrive, but the receiver cannot expose them through that stream until the missing earlier bytes are recovered. This is **head-of-line blocking**.

Ordering is often exactly what we want. The trouble is imposing one ordering on unrelated work. Captions may be useful even while an old video frame is being repaired.

## Independent streams

QUIC provides multiple reliable, ordered byte streams within one connection. Loss affecting one stream does not impose that stream’s delivery order on another. A stream still has its own ordering: later bytes in that same stream wait for missing earlier bytes.

A byte stream has no built-in message boundaries. If the publisher writes two objects, the receiver cannot assume two reads will return those two objects. MOQT supplies framing so the receiver can find where each object starts and ends. [RFC 9000 §2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-2.2) explains this distinction.

The independence is not unlimited. Streams still compete for connection bandwidth, and connection-level flow control can constrain them together. QUIC removes a particular delivery dependency; it does not give every stream a private network.

QUIC applies flow-control limits to both individual streams and their combined data. A receiver that stops consuming one stream can therefore hold up other streams if the connection-wide limit is exhausted. See [RFC 9000 §4.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-4.1) and [RFC 9002 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002.html#section-7).

MoQ takes advantage of this distinction by putting independently useful content on different streams. The grouping decisions above the transport determine how useful that independence becomes.

## What a lost packet holds up

Suppose camera bytes use stream A and captions use stream B. The offsets below are illustrative byte positions, not MoQ object IDs.

| Event | Stream A: camera | Stream B: captions |
|---|---|---|
| Packet 10 arrives | Bytes 0–99 are readable | No data yet |
| Packet 11 is lost | Bytes 100–199 are missing | No data in this packet |
| Packet 12 arrives | Bytes 200–299 wait behind the gap | Bytes 0–39 can be read |
| Missing data arrives in a later packet | Bytes 100–299 become readable in order | No need to wait for A's repair |

This is the benefit of separate stream ordering. If the lost packet had carried data from both streams, both could have gaps. Congestion feedback can also slow the whole connection. Stream independence does not mean immunity to the same network failure.

## Reliability can have an ending

Reliable delivery means lost stream bytes can be retransmitted. It does not mean the application must keep a stream alive forever. A sender can reset a stream; a receiver can ask it to stop. That gives a live application a way to abandon work.

Consider an old camera group that is still incomplete when a fresh independent group becomes available. Continuing to repair the old group may improve completeness, but delay the picture the viewer wants now. Cancelling old work is an application decision enabled by the transport.

## Where datagrams fit

QUIC’s DATAGRAM extension provides messages that are not retransmitted by QUIC when lost. They share the connection’s security and congestion control. They do not promise arrival or ordering, and their size is constrained by the path and negotiated limits.

QUIC does not split a DATAGRAM frame across packets. If an application’s message is too large, it must choose another mapping or define its own fragmentation and reassembly. That also means deciding what to do when one fragment is missing. See [RFC 9221 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9221.html#section-5).

That can suit a small, replaceable sensor update. It is less convenient for a large video frame that cannot fit in a datagram. A protocol must define how content maps onto these tools; “uses UDP” alone says very little about reliability.

A QUIC datagram is also different from a UDP packet. QUIC adds its own framing, encryption, and congestion behavior on top of UDP.

## Security belongs to the connection

Running over UDP does not mean sending plaintext. QUIC uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, the security protocol also used by HTTPS, to authenticate the server and establish keys that protect packets. With a relay in the middle, the publisher-to-relay and relay-to-viewer connections have separate protection. Hiding the content from the relay itself requires another layer, which we will discuss in the security chapter. See [RFC 9001 §4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html#section-4).

## WebTransport is the browser doorway

Browser JavaScript does not generally get a raw QUIC socket. **WebTransport** exposes streams and datagrams to web applications. For the MOQT mapping described in this edition, the browser uses WebTransport over HTTP/3; native software can use QUIC directly.

| Layer, from the application toward the network | Native direct-QUIC path | Browser path used in this book |
|---|---|---|
| Content and requests | MoQ Transport | MoQ Transport |
| Browser session interface | Not needed | WebTransport over HTTP/3 |
| Multiplexed secure transport | QUIC, integrating TLS 1.3 | QUIC, integrating TLS 1.3 |
| Datagram transport | UDP | UDP |
| Network addressing and forwarding | IP | IP |

**HTTP/3** is HTTP mapped onto QUIC. Using WebTransport over HTTP/3 does not mean making a new HTTP request for every media object. Once established, the WebTransport session exposes streams and datagrams for the application. See [RFC 9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html) and the [WebTransport API specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/webtransport/).

WebTransport transports application bytes. It does not know that those bytes represent a subscription, an Opus packet, or a camera frame. A MoQ implementation still has to implement the protocol above it.

## A fallback changes the tradeoffs

The moq.dev stack documents a WebSocket fallback. This can help reach networks where the preferred transport is unavailable. It does not preserve all of QUIC’s independent-stream behavior: TCP provides one reliable, ordered byte stream. When the fallback carries all its work over that stream, missing bytes can hold up later bytes belonging to unrelated work.

When testing a player, record which transport it actually used. Otherwise, you can spend a long time explaining “QUIC performance” while measuring a different path.

For a first mental model, keep three questions separate: can the client connect, can the peers speak the same MoQ version, and can the receiver use the content? Each can fail while the previous one succeeds.

## Reading a QUIC packet

The rest of this chapter looks inside the transport. You can continue to [Tracks, Groups and Objects](../03-tracks-groups-and-objects/index.qmd) now and return here when you want to read packet fields.

A **QUIC frame** is a transport instruction inside a QUIC packet. It is unrelated to a video frame, which represents a picture. A packet can carry several QUIC frames, including stream data from different streams.

| QUIC frame | What it carries | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `STREAM` | Stream ID, byte offset, and data; optionally an end marker | Places received bytes within the right stream |
| `ACK` | Ranges of received packet numbers | Gives the sender delivery feedback |
| `CRYPTO` | Cryptographic handshake data | Establishes the connection's security |
| `MAX_DATA` / `MAX_STREAM_DATA` | Connection / stream flow-control limits | Allows more stream bytes to be sent |
| `RESET_STREAM` | An error code and final size for an abandoned sending direction | Ends that direction without delivering every byte |
| `STOP_SENDING` | A request to stop a stream's sending direction | Lets a receiver reject further work |
| `DATAGRAM` | An unreliable message, when the extension is negotiated | Carries data without stream ordering or retransmission |

This is a reading guide, not a complete wire-format table. Field encodings and permitted frame combinations are defined in [RFC 9000 §19](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-19); `DATAGRAM` is defined separately in [RFC 9221](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9221.html).

Three numbers answer different questions: a **packet number** identifies a transmission within its packet-number space; a **stream ID** identifies a stream; a **byte offset** locates data within that stream. When lost stream data is sent again, it travels in a new packet, with a new packet number. It retains its position in the stream. See [RFC 9000 §13.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-13.3) for how QUIC retransmits information.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  accTitle: From a MoQ object to network packets
  accDescr: A MoQ object is framed into stream bytes. Parts of the stream are carried in QUIC STREAM frames, which travel inside QUIC packets, UDP datagrams, and IP packets. These boundaries need not align.
  O["MoQ object: metadata and payload"] --> B["Bytes on a QUIC stream"]
  B --> F["STREAM frames: stream ID, offset, bytes"]
  F --> Q["QUIC packets: frames and packet protection"]
  Q --> U["UDP datagrams"]
  U --> I["IP packets across the network"]
```

This diagram shows the direct-QUIC stream mapping. One object can span many packets; one packet can contain bytes from more than one object. The receiver reconstructs stream bytes before the MoQ parser reconstructs objects. WebTransport adds its own session and stream framing above QUIC.

### Inside the packet

The following view expands one illustrative IP packet. Boxes show containment, not bit widths. Here, one UDP datagram contains one QUIC packet; other valid arrangements can carry multiple QUIC packets in a datagram.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Nested structure of a packet carrying QUIC stream data
    accDescr: An IP packet contains an IP header and a UDP datagram. The UDP datagram contains its header and a QUIC packet. The QUIC packet has a header and protected payload. After decryption the payload contains frames, including a STREAM frame with a stream ID, offset, and application bytes.
    subgraph IP["IP packet"]
      IH["IP header: addresses and network fields"]
      subgraph UDP["UDP datagram"]
        UH["UDP header: ports, length, checksum"]
        subgraph QUIC["QUIC packet"]
          QH["QUIC header: packet type information, connection ID, packet number"]
          subgraph P["Protected payload — logical contents after decryption"]
            ACK["ACK frame"]
            STREAM["STREAM frame: stream ID, offset, data"]
          end
        end
      end
    end
```

The header's form depends on the packet type. A connection ID helps identify a connection; a stream ID appears inside a `STREAM` frame and identifies one stream within it. The frame's data can hold only part of a MoQ object.

For 1-RTT packets on a QUIC v1 connection, the short-header layout is more compact:

| Field, in wire order | Size | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| First byte | 8 bits | Header form, fixed bit, spin bit, reserved bits, key phase, packet-number length |
| Destination connection ID | Agreed length; possibly zero | Identifies the receiving connection |
| Packet number | 1–4 bytes | Encodes a packet number for reconstruction by the receiver |
| Protected payload | Remaining bytes | Encrypted frames and authentication tag |

Selected first-byte bits and the packet-number bytes have **header protection**. The payload has authenticated encryption. A packet capture therefore does not expose this logical frame view without the relevant keys. Long headers, used by Initial and Handshake packets, also carry a version and source connection ID. Read [RFC 9000 §17](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-17) for the exact layouts and [RFC 9001 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html#section-5) for protection.


### Read the first byte, bit by bit

Here is the base QUIC v1 short header **before header protection is applied**. It assumes no extension changes these bits. Read the first row from the most significant bit to the least significant bit. The remaining rows show field order; their drawn widths are not proportional to their lengths.

```{=html}
<figure class="wire-format">
<table aria-label="QUIC version 1 short header bit layout">
<thead><tr><th>Bit 7</th><th>6</th><th>5</th><th>4</th><th>3</th><th>2</th><th>1</th><th>0</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>0<br><small>Form</small></td><td>1<br><small>Fixed</small></td><td>S<br><small>Spin</small></td><td colspan="2">00<br><small>Reserved</small></td><td>K<br><small>Key phase</small></td><td colspan="2">PP<br><small>Packet-number length</small></td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="8">Destination connection ID <small>— length known from connection context; may be zero</small></td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="8">Packet number <small>— 1, 2, 3, or 4 bytes</small></td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="8">Protected payload <small>— encrypted frames and authentication tag</small></td></tr>
</tbody></table>
<figcaption>QUIC v1 short header. Header protection masks the reserved bits, key-phase bit, packet-number-length bits, and packet-number bytes.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

`PP` encodes the packet-number length minus one: `00` means one byte; `11` means four. The spin bit supports optional passive latency measurement. The key-phase bit helps identify packet-protection key updates. The short header has no version field or connection-ID-length field; decoding requires connection context. See [RFC 9000 §17.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-17.3.1).

The optional [QUIC-bit extension, RFC 9287 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9287.html#section-3), allows peers to vary the otherwise fixed bit after the required negotiation. The layout above follows RFC 9000 without that extension.

For example, first byte `0x41` is binary `01000001`: short header, fixed bit set, spin zero, reserved zero, key phase zero, and a two-byte packet number. This is the unprotected value. You cannot apply that reading directly to a protected packet capture.

### How variable-length integers work

Many QUIC frame fields use a **variable-length integer**, abbreviated *varint*. The first two bits say how many bytes belong to the integer; the remaining bits carry its value, most significant bytes first.

| Prefix bits | Total bytes | Value bits | Largest value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `00` | 1 | 6 | 63 |
| `01` | 2 | 14 | 16,383 |
| `10` | 4 | 30 | 1,073,741,823 |
| `11` | 8 | 62 | 4,611,686,018,427,387,903 |

A one-byte value of 37 is `0x25`. The value 64 needs at least two bytes: `0x40 0x40`. Remove the leading `01` length prefix, then interpret the remaining 14 bits as the value. This encoding is defined in [RFC 9000 §16](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-16). Packet numbers use a different encoding; do not parse them as varints.

### Decode one STREAM frame

A `STREAM` frame type is in the range `0x08`–`0x0f`. Its low three bits control which fields follow:

| Flag | Mask | When set |
|---|---|---|
| OFF | `0x04` | An Offset field is present; otherwise the offset is zero |
| LEN | `0x02` | A Length field is present; otherwise data extends to the packet's end |
| FIN | `0x01` | These bytes end the stream's sending direction |

```{=html}
<figure class="wire-format">
<table aria-label="QUIC STREAM frame fields in wire order">
<thead><tr><th>Type</th><th>Stream ID</th><th>Offset</th><th>Length</th><th>Data</th></tr></thead>
<tbody><tr><td>Varint<br><small>0x08–0x0f</small></td><td>Varint<br><small>Always</small></td><td>Varint<br><small>Only if OFF = 1</small></td><td>Varint<br><small>Only if LEN = 1</small></td><td>Bytes<br><small>Application content</small></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<figcaption>STREAM frame layout after packet decryption. Each variable-length field changes where the next field begins.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

Try this complete illustrative frame, shown **after decryption**:

```{=html}
<figure class="wire-format byte-example">
<table aria-label="Decoded STREAM frame: seven bytes with field annotations">
<thead><tr><th>Byte 0</th><th>Byte 1</th><th>Byte 2</th><th>Byte 3</th><th>Byte 4</th><th>Byte 5</th><th>Byte 6</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr class="hex-values"><td>0e</td><td>02</td><td>00</td><td>03</td><td>61</td><td>62</td><td>63</td></tr>
<tr><td>Type<small>STREAM</small></td><td>Stream ID<small>2</small></td><td>Offset<small>0</small></td><td>Length<small>3 bytes</small></td><td colspan="3">Data<small>“abc”</small></td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="4">Frame metadata<small>OFF = 1, LEN = 1, FIN = 0</small></td><td colspan="3">Application bytes<small>Stream offsets 0, 1, 2</small></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption>Read left to right. Each cell in the hexadecimal row is one byte. The first four describe the frame; the last three carry its data. Values are shown after decryption.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

Every integer in this example fits in one byte. Stream 2 is a client-initiated unidirectional stream. These three bytes occupy offsets 0, 1, and 2; FIN is unset, so the frame does not end the stream. This is a QUIC example, not a valid MoQ message: `abc` is just recognizable test data. Exact frame rules appear in [RFC 9000 §19.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-19.8), with stream IDs in [§2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-2.1).


### The handshake, message by message

A **handshake** establishes the shared state needed for protected communication. This example shows a fresh QUIC connection with server authentication, without Retry, resumption, or packet loss. Each arrow represents a flight of messages; it need not fit in one packet.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A fresh QUIC connection using TLS 1.3
    accDescr: The client sends ClientHello in Initial packets. The server sends ServerHello in Initial packets and its certificate and Finished in Handshake packets. The client verifies the server and sends Finished. The server confirms the handshake with HANDSHAKE_DONE.
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: Initial: CRYPTO carrying ClientHello
    S->>C: Initial: CRYPTO carrying ServerHello
    S->>C: Handshake: encrypted extensions, certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished
    Note over C: Verify server identity and handshake
    C->>S: Handshake: CRYPTO carrying Finished
    Note over S: Verify client Finished
    S->>C: 1-RTT: HANDSHAKE_DONE
    C->>S: 1-RTT: application frames
    S->>C: 1-RTT: application frames
```

The handshake messages shown here travel in QUIC `CRYPTO` frames. QUIC performs packet protection rather than carrying TLS records as TCP-based TLS does. `Initial`, `Handshake`, and `1-RTT` identify packet protection levels; they are not three separate connections. The server's certificate authenticates the server, not the student's permission to watch a lecture. See [RFC 9001 §4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html#section-4).

Initial packets use publicly derivable protection keys, so a network observer can recover their contents. Handshake and 1-RTT packets use secret keys established through TLS. Do not confuse Initial packet protection with confidentiality; see [RFC 9001 §5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001.html#section-5).

The drawing puts application traffic last for readability. Endpoints can begin sending 1-RTT data once the required keys are available; the client need not wait for `HANDSHAKE_DONE` before sending it. ACKs are omitted. Resumption can enable **0-RTT**, or early data, with replay considerations that applications must handle. The complete flows appear in [RFC 9000 §7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-7.1).
